verses.zh: 非斯都既然定规了，叫我们坐船往意大利去，便将保罗和别的囚犯交给御营里的一个百夫长，名叫犹流。
verses.en: When it was decided we[NOTE:1] would sail to Italy,[NOTE:2] they handed over Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion[NOTE:3] of the Augustan Cohort[NOTE:4] named Julius.
notes: This marks the beginning of one of the “we” sections in Acts (16:10-17; 20:5-15; 21:1-18; 27:1-28:16). These have been traditionally understood to mean that the author was in the company of Paul for this part of the journey.

Sail to Italy. This voyage with its difficulty serves to show how God protected Paul on his long journey to Rome. From the perspective of someone in Palestine, this may well picture “the end of the earth” quite literally (cf. Acts 1:8).
See the note on the word centurion in 10:1.

The Augustan Cohort. A cohort was a Roman military unit of about 600 soldiers, one-tenth of a legion. There is considerable debate over the identification of this particular cohort and the meaning of the title Augustan mentioned here. These may well have been auxiliary (provincial) troops given the honorary title.tn According to BDAG 917 s.v. σεβαστός, “In σπεῖρα Σεβαστή 27:1 (cp. OGI 421) Σεβαστή is likew. an exact transl. of Lat. Augusta, an honorary title freq. given to auxiliary troops (Ptolem. renders it Σεβαστή in connection w. three legions that bore it: 2, 3, 30; 2, 9, 18; 4, 3, 30) imperial cohort.” According to W. Foerster (TDNT 7:175), “In Ac. 27:1 the σπεῖρα Σεβαστή is an expression also found elsewhere for ‘auxiliary troops.’” In no case would this refer to a special imperial bodyguard, and to translate “imperial regiment” or “imperial cohort” might give this impression. There is some archaeological evidence for a Cohors Augusta I stationed in Syria during the time of Augustus, but whether this is the same unit is very debatable.

verses.zh: 有一只亚大米田的船，要沿着亚细亚一带地方的海边走，我们就上了那船开行；有马其顿的帖撒罗尼迦人亚里达古和我们同去。
verses.en: We went on board[NOTE:1] a ship from Adramyttium[NOTE:2] that was about to sail to various ports[NOTE:3] along the coast of the province of Asia[NOTE:4] and put out to sea,[NOTE:5] accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian[NOTE:6] from Thessalonica.[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “Going on board.” The participle ἐπιβάντες (epibantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Adramyttium was a seaport in Mysia on the western coast of Asia Minor.
Grk “places.”

Grk “Asia”; in the NT this always refers to the Roman province of Asia. The Roman province of Asia made up about one-third of modern Asia Minor and was on the western side of it. Asia lay to the west of the region of Phrygia and Galatia. The words “the province of” are supplied to indicate to the modern reader that this does not refer to the continent of Asia.

Although not explicitly stated, the ship put out to sea from the port of Caesarea (where the previous events had taken place (cf. 25:13) and then sailed along the Asiatic coast (the first stop was Sidon, v. 3).tn BDAG 62 s.v. ἀνάγω 4 states, “as a nautical t.t. (ἀ. τὴν ναῦν put a ship to sea), mid. or pass. ἀνάγεσθαι to begin to go by boat, put out to sea.”
A Macedonian. The city of Thessalonica (modern Salonica) was in the Roman province of Macedonia in Greece.
For location see JP1-C1; JP2-C1; JP3-C1; JP4-C1.

verses.zh: 第二天，到了西顿；犹流宽待保罗，准他往朋友那里去，受他们的照应。
verses.en: The next day we put in[NOTE:1] at Sidon,[NOTE:2] and Julius, treating Paul kindly,[NOTE:3] allowed him to go to his friends so they could provide him with what he needed.[NOTE:4]
notes: BDAG 516 s.v. κατάγω states, “Hence the pass., in act. sense, of ships and seafarers put in εἴς τι at a harbor…εἰς Σιδῶνα Ac 27:3.”
For location see Map1-A1; JP3-F3; JP4-F3.sn Sidon is another seaport 75 mi (120 km) north of Caesarea.

Treating Paul kindly. Paul’s treatment followed the pattern of the earlier imprisonment (cf. Acts 24:23).tn BDAG 1056 s.v. φιλανθρώπως states, “benevolently, kindly φιλανθρώπως χρῆσθαί (τινι) treat someone in kindly fashion…Ac 27:3.”
Grk “to go to his friends to be cared for.” The scene is an indication of Christian hospitality.

verses.zh: 从那里又开船，因为风不顺，就贴着塞浦路斯背风岸行去。
verses.en: From there we put out to sea[NOTE:1] and sailed under the lee[NOTE:2] of Cyprus because the winds were against us.
notes: Grk “putting out to sea.” The participle ἀναχθέντες (anachthentes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. BDAG 62 s.v. ἀνάγω 4 states, “as a nautical t.t. (ἀ. τὴν ναῦν put a ship to sea), mid. or pass. ἀνάγεσθαι to begin to go by boat, put out to sea.”
BDAG 1040 s.v. ὑποπλέω states, “sail under the lee of an island, i.e. in such a way that the island protects the ship fr. the wind Ac 27:4, 7.” Thus they were east and north of the island.

verses.zh: 过了基利家、旁非利亚前面的海，就到了吕家的每拉。
verses.en: After we had sailed across the open sea[NOTE:1] off Cilicia and Pamphylia,[NOTE:2] we put in[NOTE:3] at Myra[NOTE:4] in Lycia.[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “the depths,” the deep area of a sea far enough from land that it is not protected by the coast (L&N 1.73).
Pamphylia was a province in the southern part of Asia Minor; it was west of Cilicia (see BDAG 753 s.v. Παμφυλία).
BDAG 531 s.v. κατέρχομαι 2 states, “Of ships and those who sail in them, who ‘come down’ fr. the ‘high seas’: arrive, put in…ἔις τι at someth. a harbor 18:22; 21:3; 27:5.”
Myra was a city on the southern coast of Lycia in Asia Minor. This journey from Sidon (v. 3) was 440 mi (700 km) and took about 15 days.
Lycia was the name of a peninsula on the southern coast of Asia Minor between Caria and Pamphylia.

verses.zh: 在那里，百夫长遇见一只亚历山大的船，要往意大利去，便叫我们上了那船。
verses.en: There the centurion[NOTE:1] found[NOTE:2] a ship from Alexandria[NOTE:3] sailing for Italy, and he put us aboard it.
notes: See the note on the word centurion in 10:1.
Grk “finding.” The participle εὑρών (heurōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

Alexandria (modern Alexandria) was a great city of northern Egypt which was a center for grain trade to Rome. Therefore this type of travel connection was common at the time. For a winter journey (considered hazardous) there were special bonuses and insurance provided (Suetonius, Life of Claudius 18.1-2).

verses.zh: 一连多日，船行得慢，仅仅来到革尼土的对面。因为被风拦阻，就贴着克里特背风岸，从撒摩尼对面行过。
verses.en: We sailed slowly[NOTE:1] for many days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus.[NOTE:2] Because the wind prevented us from going any farther,[NOTE:3] we sailed under the lee[NOTE:4] of Crete off Salmone.[NOTE:5]
notes: The participle βραδυπλοοῦντες (braduploountes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Cnidus was the name of a peninsula on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor. This was about 130 mi (210 km) from Myra.

This genitive absolute construction with προσεῶντος (proseōntos) has been translated as a causal adverbial participle. L&N 13.139 translates the phrase μὴ προσεῶντος ἡμᾶς τοῦ ἀνέμου (mē proseōntos hēmas tou anemou) as “the wind would not let us go any farther.”
BDAG 1040 s.v. ὑποπλέω states, “sail under the lee of an island, i.e. in such a way that the island protects the ship fr. the wind Ac 27:4, 7.”
Salmone was the name of a promontory on the northeastern corner of the island of Crete. This was about 100 mi (160 km) farther along.

verses.zh: 我们沿岸行走，仅仅来到一个地方，名叫佳澳；离那里不远，有拉西亚城。
verses.en: With difficulty we sailed along the coast[NOTE:1] of Crete[NOTE:2] and came to a place called Fair Havens that was near the town of Lasea.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “sailing along the coast…we came.” The participle παραλεγόμενοι (paralegomenoi) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. L&N 54.8, “παραλέγομαι: (a technical, nautical term) to sail along beside some object—‘to sail along the coast, to sail along the shore.’…‘they sailed along the coast of Crete’ Ac 27:13.”
Grk “it”; the referent (Crete) has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Lasea was a city on the southern coast of the island of Crete. This was about 60 mi (96 km) farther.

verses.zh: 走的日子多了，已经过了禁食的节期，行船又危险，保罗就劝众人说：
verses.en: Since considerable time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous[NOTE:1] because the fast[NOTE:2] was already over,[NOTE:3] Paul advised them,[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “unsafe” (BDAG 383 s.v. ἐπισφαλής). The term is a NT hapax legomenon.

The fast refers to the Jewish Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur. It was now into October and the dangerous winter winds would soon occur (Suetonius, Life of Claudius 18; Josephus, J. W. 1.14.2-3 [1.279-281]).

The accusative articular infinitive παρεληλυθέναι (parelēluthenai) after the preposition διά (dia) is causal. BDAG 776 s.v. παρέρχομαι 2 has “διὰ τὸ τὴν νηστείαν ἤδη παρεληλυθέναι because the fast was already over Ac 27:9.”

Paul advised them. A literary theme surfaces here: Though Paul is under arrest, he will be the one to guide them all through the dangers of the storm and shipwreck, showing clearly God’s presence and protection of him. The story is told in great detail. This literary effect of slowing down the passage of time and narrating with many details serves to add a sense of drama to the events described.tn Grk “Paul advised, saying to them.” The participle λέγων (legōn) is redundant in English and has not been translated. On the term translated “advised,” see BDAG 764 s.v. παραινέω, which usually refers to recommendations.

verses.zh: 「众位，我看这次行船，不但货物和船要受伤损，大遭破坏，连我们的性命也难保。」
verses.en: “Men, I can see the voyage is going to end[NOTE:1] in disaster[NOTE:2] and great loss not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “is going to be with disaster.”
Or “hardship,” “damage.” BDAG 1022 s.v. ὕβρις 3 states, “fig. hardship, disaster, damage caused by the elements…w. ζημία Ac 27:10.”
Grk “souls” (here, one’s physical life).

verses.zh: 但百夫长信从掌船的和船主，不信从保罗所说的。
verses.en: But the centurion[NOTE:1] was more convinced[NOTE:2] by the captain[NOTE:3] and the ship’s owner than by what Paul said.[NOTE:4]
notes: See the note on the word centurion in 10:1.
Or “persuaded.”

BDAG 456 s.v. κυβερνήτης 1 has “one who is responsible for the management of a ship, shipmaster…W. ναύκληρος, the ‘shipowner’…Ac 27:11” See further L. Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World, 316-18.

More convinced by the captain and the ship’s owner than by what Paul said. The position taken by the centurion was logical, since he was following “professional” advice. But this was not a normal voyage.tn Grk “than by what was said by Paul.” The passive construction has been converted to an active one to simplify the translation.

verses.zh: 且因在这海口过冬不便，船上的人就多半说，不如开船离开这地方，或者能到菲尼基过冬。菲尼基是克里特的一个海口，一面朝东北，一面朝东南。
verses.en: Because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided[NOTE:1] to put out to sea[NOTE:2] from there. They hoped that[NOTE:3] somehow they could reach[NOTE:4] Phoenix,[NOTE:5] a harbor of Crete facing[NOTE:6] southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there.
notes: BDAG 181-82 s.v. βουλή 2.a, “β. τίθεσθαι (Judg 19:30; Ps 12:3) decide 27:12 (w. inf. foll.).”
BDAG 62 s.v. ἀνάγω 4, “as a nautical t.t. (ἀ. τὴν ναῦν put a ship to sea), mid. or pass. ἀνάγεσθαι to begin to go by boat, put out to sea.”

Grk “from there, if somehow” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was begun here in the translation and the introductory phrase “They hoped that” supplied (with the subject, “they,” repeated from the previous clause) to make a complete English sentence.
Grk “if somehow, reaching Phoenix, they could…” The participle καταντήσαντες (katantēsantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Phoenix was a seaport on the southern coast of the island of Crete. This was about 30 mi (48 km) farther west.
Or “a harbor of Crete open to the southwest and northwest.”

verses.zh: 这时，微微起了南风，他们以为得意，就起了锚，贴近克里特行去。
verses.en: When a gentle south wind sprang up, they thought[NOTE:1] they could carry out[NOTE:2] their purpose, so they weighed anchor[NOTE:3] and sailed close along the coast[NOTE:4] of Crete.
notes: Grk “thinking.” The participle δόξαντες (doxantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

Or “accomplish.” L&N 68.29, for κρατέω, has “to be able to complete or finish, presumably despite difficulties—‘to accomplish, to do successfully, to carry out.’…‘thinking that they could carry out their purpose’ Ac 27:13.”
Or “departed.”

L&N 54.8, “παραλέγομαι: (a technical, nautical term) to sail along beside some object—‘to sail along the coast, to sail along the shore.’…‘they sailed along the coast of Crete’ Ac 27:13.” With the addition of the adverb ἆσσον (asson) this becomes “sailed close along the coast of Crete.”

verses.zh: 不多几时，狂风从岛上扑下来；那风名叫「友拉革罗」。
verses.en: Not long after this, a hurricane-force[NOTE:1] wind called the northeaster[NOTE:2] blew down from the island.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “a wind like a typhoon.” That is, a very violent wind like a typhoon or hurricane (BDAG 1021 s.v. τυφωνικός).
Or called Euraquilo (the actual name of the wind, a sailor’s term which was a combination of Greek and Latin). According to Strabo (Geography 1.2.21), this was a violent northern wind.
Grk “from it”; the referent (the island) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 船被风抓住，敌不住风，我们就任风刮去。
verses.en: When the ship was caught in it[NOTE:1] and could not head into[NOTE:2] the wind, we gave way to it and were driven[NOTE:3] along.
notes: Or “was forced off course.” Grk “The ship being caught in it.” The genitive absolute construction with the participle συναρπασθέντος (sunarpasthentos) has been taken temporally; it could also be translated as causal (“Because the ship was caught in it”).

BDAG 91 s.v. ἀντοφθαλμέω states, “Metaph. of a ship τοῦ πλοίου μὴ δυναμένοι ἀ. τῷ ἀνέμῳ since the ship was not able to face the wind, i.e. with its bow headed against the forces of the waves Ac 27:15.”
Caught in the violent wind, the ship was driven along. They were now out of control, at the mercy of the wind and sea.

verses.zh: 贴着一个小岛的背风岸奔行，那岛名叫高大，在那里仅仅收住了小船。
verses.en: As we ran under the lee of[NOTE:1] a small island called Cauda,[NOTE:2] we were able with difficulty to get the ship’s boat[NOTE:3] under control.
notes: BDAG 1042 s.v. ὑποτρέχω states, “run or sail under the lee of, nautical t.t.…Ac 27:16.” The participle ὑποδραμόντες (hupodramontes) has been taken temporally (“as we ran under the lee of”). While this could also be translated as a participle of means (“by running…”) this might suggest the ship was still under a greater degree of control by its crew than it probably was.
Cauda. This island was located south of Crete, about 23 mi (36 km) from where they began. There are various ways to spell the island’s name (e.g., Clauda, BDAG 546 s.v. Κλαῦδα).

The ship’s boat was a small rowboat, normally towed behind a ship in good weather rather than stowed on board. It was used for landings, to maneuver the ship for tacking, and to lay anchors (not a lifeboat in the modern sense, although it could have served as a means of escape for some of the sailors; see v. 30). See L. Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World, 248f.

verses.zh: 既然把小船拉上来，就用缆索捆绑船底，又恐怕在赛耳底沙滩上搁了浅，就落下篷来，任船飘去。
verses.en: After the crew[NOTE:1] had hoisted it aboard,[NOTE:2] they used supports[NOTE:3] to undergird the ship. Fearing they would run aground[NOTE:4] on the Syrtis,[NOTE:5] they lowered the sea anchor,[NOTE:6] thus letting themselves be driven along.
notes: Grk “After hoisting it up, they…”; the referent (the ship’s crew) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The participle ἄραντες (arantes) has been taken temporally.
Possibly “ropes” or “cables”; Grk “helps” (a word of uncertain meaning; probably a nautical technical term, BDAG 180 s.v. βοήθεια 2).
BDAG 308 s.v. ἐκπίπτω 2 states, “drift off course, run aground, nautical term εἴς τι on someth….on the Syrtis 27:17.”

That is, on the sandbars and shallows of the Syrtis.sn On the Syrtis. The Syrtis was the name of two gulfs on the North African coast (modern Libya), feared greatly by sailors because of their shifting sandbars and treacherous shallows. The Syrtis here is the so-called Great Syrtis, toward Cyrenaica. It had a horrible reputation as a sailors’ graveyard (Pliny, Natural History 5.26). Josephus (J. W. 2.16.4 [2.381]) says the name alone struck terror in those who heard it. It was near the famous Scylla and Charybdis mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey.

Or perhaps “mainsail.” The meaning of this word is uncertain. BDAG 927 s.v. σκεῦος 1 has “τὸ σκεῦος Ac 27:17 seems to be the kedge or driving anchor” while C. Maurer (TDNT 7:362) notes, “The meaning in Ac. 27:17: χαλάσαντες τὸ σκεῦος, is uncertain. Prob. the ref. is not so much to taking down the sails as to throwing the draganchor overboard to lessen the speed of the ship.” In spite of this L&N 6.1 states, “In Ac 27:17, for example, the reference of σκεῦος is generally understood to be the mainsail.” A reference to the sail is highly unlikely because in a storm of the force described in Ac 27:14, the sail would have been taken down and reefed immediately, to prevent its being ripped to shreds or torn away by the gale.

verses.zh: 我们被风浪逼得甚急，第二天众人就把货物抛在海里。
verses.en: The next day, because we were violently battered by the storm,[NOTE:1] they began throwing the cargo overboard,[NOTE:2]
notes: BDAG 980 s.v. σφόδρῶς states, “very much, greatly, violently…σφ. χειμάζεσθαι be violently beaten by a storm Ac 27:18.”

The desperation of the sailors in throwing the cargo overboard is reminiscent of Jonah 1:5. At this point they were only concerned with saving themselves.tn Or “jettisoning [the cargo]” (a nautical technical term). The words “the cargo” are not in the Greek text but are implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.

verses.zh: 到第三天，他们又亲手把船上的器具抛弃了。
verses.en: and on the third day they threw the ship’s gear[NOTE:1] overboard with their own hands.
notes: Or “rigging,” “tackle”; Grk “the ship’s things.” Here the more abstract “gear” is preferred to “rigging” or “tackle” as a translation for σκεῦος (skeuos) because in v. 40 the sailors are still able to raise the (fore)sail, which they could not have done if the ship’s rigging or tackle had been jettisoned here.

verses.zh: 太阳和星辰多日不显露，又有狂风大浪催逼，我们得救的指望就都绝了。
verses.en: When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and a violent[NOTE:1] storm continued to batter us,[NOTE:2] we finally abandoned all hope of being saved.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “no small storm” = a very great storm.

Grk “no small storm pressing on us.” The genitive absolute construction with the participle ἐπικειμένου (epikeimenou) has been translated as parallel to the previous genitive absolute construction (which was translated as temporal). BDAG 373 s.v. ἐπίκειμαι 2.b states, “of impersonal force confront χειμῶνος ἐπικειμένου since a storm lay upon us Ac 27:20.” L&N 14.2, “‘the stormy weather did not abate in the least’ or ‘the violent storm continued’ Ac 27:20.” To this last was added the idea of “battering” from the notion of “pressing upon” inherent in ἐπίκειμαι (epikeimai).

Grk “finally all hope that we would be saved was abandoned.” The passive construction has been converted to an active one to simplify the translation. This represents a clearly secular use of the term σῴζω (sōzō) in that it refers to deliverance from the storm. At this point those on board the ship gave up hope of survival.

verses.zh: 众人多日没有吃甚么，保罗就出来站在他们中间，说：「众位，你们本该听我的话，不离开克里特，免得遭这样的伤损破坏。
verses.en: Since many of them had no desire to eat,[NOTE:1] Paul[NOTE:2] stood up[NOTE:3] among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me[NOTE:4] and not put out to sea[NOTE:5] from Crete, thus avoiding[NOTE:6] this damage and loss.
notes: Or “Since they had no desire to eat for a long time.” The genitive absolute construction with the participle ὑπαρχούσης (huparchousēs) has been translated as a causal adverbial participle. It could also be translated temporally (“When many of them had no desire to eat”). The translation of πολλῆς (pollēs) as a substantized adjective referring to the people on board the ship (“many of them”) rather than a period of time (“for a long time”; so most modern versions) follows BDAG 143 s.v. ἀσιτία, which has “πολλῆς ἀ. ὑπαρχούσης since almost nobody wanted to eat because of anxiety or seasickness…Ac 27:21.” This detail indicates how turbulent things were on board the ship.
Here τότε (tote) is redundant (pleonastic) according to BDAG 1012-13 s.v. τότε 2; thus it has not been translated.
Grk “standing up…said.” The participle σταθείς (statheis) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

L&N 36.12 has “πειθαρχήσαντάς μοι μὴ ἀνάγεσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς Κρήτης ‘you should have listened to me and not have sailed from Crete’ Ac 27:21.”sn By saying “you should have listened to me and not put out to sea from Crete” Paul was not “rubbing it in,” but was reasserting his credibility before giving his next recommendation.
BDAG 62 s.v. ἀνάγω 4, “as a nautical t.t. (ἀ. τὴν ναῦν put a ship to sea), mid. or pass. ἀνάγεσθαι to begin to go by boat, put out to sea.”
The infinitive κερδῆσαι (kerdēsai) has been translated as resultative.

verses.zh: 现在我还劝你们放心，你们的性命一个也不失丧，惟独失丧这船。
verses.en: And now I advise[NOTE:1] you to keep up your courage, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only the ship will be lost.[NOTE:2]
notes: The same verb is used for Paul’s original recommendation in Ac 27:9.

The “prophecy” about the ship serves to underscore Paul’s credibility as an agent of God. Paul addressed his audience carefully and drew attention to the sovereign knowledge of God.tn Grk “except the ship.” Here “but” is used to translate the improper preposition πλήν (plēn; see BDAG 826 s.v. πλήν 2) since an exception like this, where two different categories of objects are involved (people and a ship), is more naturally expressed in contemporary English with an adversative (“but”). The words “will be lost” are also supplied for clarity.

verses.zh: 因我所属所事奉的　神，他的使者昨夜站在我旁边，说：
verses.en: For last night an angel of the God to whom I belong[NOTE:1] and whom I serve[NOTE:2] came to me[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “of whom I am.” The relative clause was translated following L&N 15.86 s.v. παρίσταμαι.
Or “worship.”
Or “stood by me.” BDAG 778 s.v. παρίστημι/παριστάνω 2.a.α states, “approach, come τινί (to) someone…Ac 9:39; 27:23.”

verses.zh: 『保罗，不要害怕，你必定站在凯撒面前，并且与你同船的人，　神都赐给你了。』
verses.en: and said,[NOTE:1] ‘Do not be afraid, Paul! You must stand before[NOTE:2] Caesar,[NOTE:3] and God has graciously granted you the safety[NOTE:4] of all who are sailing with you.’
notes: Grk “came to me saying.” The participle λέγων (legōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

BDAG 778 s.v. παρίστημι/παριστάνω 2.a.α states, “Also as a t.t. of legal usage appear before, come before…Καίσαρι σε δεῖ παραστῆναι you must stand before the Emperor (as judge) Ac 27:24.” See Acts 23:11. Luke uses the verb δεῖ (dei) to describe what must occur.
Or “before the emperor” (“Caesar” is a title for the Roman emperor).

Grk “God has graciously granted you all who are sailing with you.” The words “the safety of” have been supplied to clarify the meaning of the verb κεχάρισται (kecharistai) in this context.sn The safety of all who are sailing with you. In a sense, Paul’s presence protects them all. For Luke, it serves as a picture of what the gospel does through Christ and through the one who brings the message.

verses.zh: 所以众位可以放心，我信　神他怎样对我说，事情也要怎样成就。
verses.en: Therefore keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God[NOTE:1] that it will be just as I have been told.
notes: BDAG 817 s.v. πιστεύω 1.c states, “w. pers. and thing added π. τινί τι believe someone with regard to someth….W. dat. of pers. and ὅτι foll…. πιστεύετέ μοι ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ πατρί J 14:11a. Cf. 4:21; Ac 27:25.”

verses.zh: 只是我们必要撞在一个岛上。」
verses.en: But we must[NOTE:1] run aground on some island.”
notes: This is another use of δεῖ (dei) to indicate necessity (see also v. 24). Acts 28:1 shows the fulfillment of this.

verses.zh: 到了第十四天夜间，船在亚得里亚海飘来飘去。约到半夜，水手以为渐近旱地，
verses.en: When the fourteenth night had come, while we were being driven[NOTE:1] across the Adriatic Sea,[NOTE:2] about midnight the sailors suspected they were approaching some land.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here “being driven” has been used to translate διαφέρω (diapherō) rather than “drifting,” because it is clear from the attempt to drop anchors in v. 29 that the ship is still being driven by the gale. “Drifting” implies lack of control, but not necessarily rapid movement.
The Adriatic Sea. They were now somewhere between Crete and Malta.

Grk “suspected that some land was approaching them.” BDAG 876 s.v. προσάγω 2.a states, “lit. ὑπενόουν προσάγειν τινά αὐτοῖς χώραν they suspected that land was near (lit. ‘approaching them’) Ac 27:27.” Current English idiom would speak of the ship approaching land rather than land approaching the ship.

verses.zh: 就探深浅，探得有十二丈；稍往前行，又探深浅，探得有九丈。
verses.en: They took soundings[NOTE:1] and found the water was twenty fathoms[NOTE:2] deep; when they had sailed a little farther[NOTE:3] they took soundings again and found it was fifteen fathoms[NOTE:4] deep.
notes: Grk “Heaving the lead, they found.” The participle βολίσαντες (bolisantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. See also BDAG 180 s.v. βολίζω. Although the term is used twice in this verse (and thus is technically not a NT hapax legomenon), it occurs nowhere else in the NT.

A fathom is about 6 feet or just under 2 meters (originally the length of a man’s outstretched arms). This was a nautical technical term for measuring the depth of water. Here it was about 120 ft (36 m).
L&N 15.12, “βραχὺ δὲ διαστήσαντες ‘when they had gone a little farther’ Ac 27:28.”
Here the depth was about 90 ft (27 m).

verses.zh: 恐怕撞在石头上，就从船尾抛下四个锚，盼望天亮。
verses.en: Because they were afraid[NOTE:1] that we would run aground on the rocky coast,[NOTE:2] they threw out[NOTE:3] four anchors from the stern and wished[NOTE:4] for day to appear.[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “fearing.” The participle φοβούμενοι (phoboumenoi) has been translated as a causal adverbial participle.
Grk “against a rough [rocky] place.” L&N 79.84 has “φοβούμενοί τε μή που κατὰ τραχεῖς τόποις ἐκπέσωμεν ‘we were afraid that we would run aground on the rocky coast’ Ac 27:29.”
Grk “throwing out…they.” The participle ῥίψαντες (rhipsantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

BDAG 417 s.v. εὔχομαι 2 states, “wish…τὶ for someth.…Foll. by acc. and inf….Ac 27:29.” The other possible meaning for this term, “pray,” is given in BDAG 417 s.v. 1 and employed by a number of translations (NAB, NRSV, NIV). If this meaning is adopted here, then “prayed for day to come” must be understood metaphorically to mean “prayed that they would live to see the day,” or “prayed that it would soon be day.”
And wished for day to appear. The sailors were hoping to hold the ship in place until morning, when they could see what was happening and where they were.tn Grk “and wished for day to come about.”

verses.zh: 水手想要逃出船去，把小船放在海里，假作要从船头抛锚的样子。
verses.en: Then when the sailors tried to escape from the ship and were lowering the ship’s boat into the sea, pretending[NOTE:1] that they were going to put out anchors from the bow,
notes: BDAG 889 s.v. πρόφασις 2 states, “προφάσει ὡς under the pretext that, pretending that…Ac 27:30.” In other words, some of the sailors gave up hope that such efforts would work and instead attempted to escape while pretending to help.

verses.zh: 保罗对百夫长和兵丁说：「这些人若不等在船上，你们必不能得救。」
verses.en: Paul said to the centurion[NOTE:1] and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay with the ship, you[NOTE:2] cannot be saved.”
notes: See the note on the word centurion in 10:1.
The pronoun you is plural in Greek.

verses.zh: 于是兵丁砍断小船的绳子，由它飘去。
verses.en: Then the soldiers cut the ropes[NOTE:1] of the ship’s boat and let it drift away.[NOTE:2]
notes: The soldiers cut the ropes. The centurion and the soldiers were now following Paul’s advice by cutting the ropes to prevent the sailors from escaping.

Or “let it fall away.” According to BDAG 308 s.v. ἐκπίπτω 1 and 2 the meaning of the verb in this verse could be either “fall away” or “drift away.” Either meaning is acceptable, and the choice between them depends almost entirely on how one reconstructs the scene. Since cutting the boat loose would in any case result in it drifting away (whether capsized or not), the meaning “drift away” as a nautical technical term has been used here.

verses.zh: 天渐亮的时候，保罗劝众人都吃饭，说：「你们悬望忍饿不吃甚么，已经十四天了。
verses.en: As day was about to dawn,[NOTE:1] Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day you have been in suspense[NOTE:2] and have gone[NOTE:3] without food; you have eaten nothing.[NOTE:4]
notes: BDAG 160 s.v. ἄχρι 1.b.α has “ἄ. οὗ ἡμέρα ἤμελλεν γίνεσθαι until the day began to dawn 27:33.”
Or “have waited anxiously.” Grk “waiting anxiously.” The participle προσδοκῶντες (prosdokōntes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Or “continued.”
Grk “having eaten nothing.” The participle προσλαβόμενοι (proslabomenoi) has been translated as a finite verb (with subject “you” supplied) due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 所以我劝你们吃饭，这是关乎你们救命的事；因为你们各人连一根头发也不至于损坏。」
verses.en: Therefore I urge you to take some food, for this is important[NOTE:1] for your survival.[NOTE:2] For not one of you will lose a hair from his head.”
notes: Or “necessary.” BDAG 873-74 s.v. πρός 1 has “πρ. τῆς σωτηρίας in the interest of safety Ac 27:34”; L&N 27.18 has “‘therefore, I urge you to take some food, for this is important for your deliverance’ or ‘…for your survival’ Ac 27:34.”
Or “deliverance” (‘salvation’ in a nontheological sense).

verses.zh: 保罗说了这话，就拿着饼，在众人面前祝谢了　神，擘开吃。
verses.en: After he said this, Paul[NOTE:1] took bread[NOTE:2] and gave thanks to God in front of them all,[NOTE:3] broke[NOTE:4] it, and began to eat.
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (Paul) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “taking bread, gave thanks.” The participle λαβών (labōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Or “before them all,” but here this could be misunderstood to indicate a temporal sequence.
Grk “and breaking it, he began.” The participle κλάσας (klasas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 于是他们都放下心，也就吃了。
verses.en: So all of them were encouraged and took food themselves.

verses.zh: 我们在船上的共有二百七十六个人。
verses.en: (We were in all 276[NOTE:1] persons on the ship.)[NOTE:2]
notes: One early ms (B) and an early version (sa) read “about seventy-six.” For discussion of how this variant probably arose, see F. F. Bruce, The Acts of the Apostles, 465.
This is a parenthetical note by the author.

verses.zh: 他们吃饱了，就把船上的麦子抛在海里，为要叫船轻一点。
verses.en: When they had eaten enough to be satisfied,[NOTE:1] they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat[NOTE:2] into the sea.
notes: Or “When they had eaten their fill.”
Or “grain.”

verses.zh: 「到了天亮，他们不认识那地方，但见一个海湾，有岸可登，就商议能把船拢进去不能。
verses.en: When day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed[NOTE:1] a bay[NOTE:2] with a beach,[NOTE:3] where they decided to run the ship aground if they could.
notes: Or “observed,” “saw.”
Or “gulf” (BDAG 557 s.v. κόλπος 3).
A beach would refer to a smooth sandy beach suitable for landing.

verses.zh: 于是砍断缆索，弃锚在海里；同时也松开舵绳，拉起头篷，顺着风向岸行去。
verses.en: So they slipped[NOTE:1] the anchors[NOTE:2] and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the linkage[NOTE:3] that bound the steering oars[NOTE:4] together. Then they hoisted[NOTE:5] the foresail[NOTE:6] to the wind and steered toward[NOTE:7] the beach.
notes: That is, released. Grk “slipping…leaving.” The participles περιελόντες (perielontes) and εἴων (eiōn) have been translated as finite verbs due to requirements of contemporary English style.
The term is used of a ship’s anchor. (BDAG 12 s.v. ἄγκυρα a).
Grk “bands”; possibly “ropes.”
Or “rudders.”
Grk “hoisting…they.” The participle ἐπάραντες (eparantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Grk “sail”; probably a reference to the foresail.
BDAG 533 s.v. κατέχω 7 states, “hold course, nautical t.t., intr….κατεῖχον εἰς τὸν αἰγιαλόν they headed for the beach Ac 27:40.”

verses.zh: 但遇着两水夹流的地方，就把船搁了浅；船头胶住不动，船尾被浪的猛力冲坏。
verses.en: But they encountered a patch of crosscurrents[NOTE:1] and ran the ship aground; the bow stuck fast and could not be moved, but the stern was being broken up by the force[NOTE:2] of the waves.
notes: Grk “fell upon a place of two seas.” The most common explanation for this term is that it refers to a reef or sandbar with the sea on both sides, as noted in BDAG 245 s.v. διθάλασσος: the “τόπος δ. Ac 27:41 is a semantic unit signifying a point (of land jutting out with water on both sides).” However, Greek had terms for a “sandbank” (θῖς [this], ταινία [tainia]), a “reef” (ἑρμα [herma]), “strait” (στενόν [stenon]), “promontory” (ἀρωτήρον [arōtēron]), and other nautical hazards, none of which are used by the author here. NEB here translates τόπον διθάλασσον (topon dithalasson) as “cross-currents,” a proposal close to that advanced by J. M. Gilchrist, “The Historicity of Paul’s Shipwreck,” JSNT 61 (1996): 29-51, who suggests the meaning is “a patch of cross-seas,” where the waves are set at an angle to the wind, a particular hazard for sailors. Thus the term most likely refers to some sort of adverse sea conditions rather than a topographical feature like a reef or sandbar.
Or “violence” (BDAG 175 s.v. βία a).

verses.zh: 兵丁的意思要把囚犯杀了，恐怕有洑水脱逃的。
verses.en: Now the soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners[NOTE:1] so that none of them would escape by swimming away.[NOTE:2]
notes: The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners. The issue here was not cruelty, but that the soldiers would be legally responsible if any prisoners escaped and would suffer punishment themselves. So they were planning to do this as an act of self-preservation. See Acts 16:27 for a similar incident.
The participle ἐκκολυμβήσας (ekkolumbēsas) has been taken instrumentally.

verses.zh: 但百夫长要救保罗，不准他们任意而行，就吩咐会洑水的，跳下水去先上岸；
verses.en: But the centurion,[NOTE:1] wanting to save Paul’s life,[NOTE:2] prevented them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land,[NOTE:3]
notes: See the note on the word centurion in 10:1.
Or “wanting to rescue Paul.”sn Thanks to the centurion who wanted to save Paul’s life, Paul was once more rescued from a potential human threat.
BDAG 347 s.v. I. ἔξειμι has “ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν get to land Ac 27:43.”

verses.zh: 其余的人可以用板子或船上的零碎东西上岸。这样，众人都得了救，上了岸。
verses.en: and the rest were to follow,[NOTE:1] some on planks[NOTE:2] and some on pieces of the ship.[NOTE:3] And in this way[NOTE:4] all were brought safely to land.
notes: The words “were to follow” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. They must be supplied to clarify the sense in contemporary English.
Or “boards” according to BDAG 913 s.v. σανίς.

Grk “on pieces from the ship”; that is, pieces of wreckage from the ship.sn Both the planks and pieces of the ship were for the weak or nonswimmers. The whole scene is a historical metaphor representing how listening to Paul and his message could save people.

Grk “And in this way it happened that.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
